abstract.p: Complex engineering systems often involve interacting transport fields in which diffusion, field-driven fluxes, production or decay, and nonlinear feedback jointly control stability, transport, and localization. Although originating in mathematical biology, the Keller–Segel system is a canonical coupled-field transport model with this structure and provides a stringent benchmark for computational methodologies aimed at complex and multiphysics transport problems. A multidimensional hybrid numerical–analytical formulation based on the Generalized Integral Transform Technique (GITT) is developed for a parabolic–parabolic Keller–Segel system with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. Spatial averages are treated analytically, zero-mean fields are expanded in normalized Neumann eigenfunctions, and exact cosine-product selection rules generate a sparse nonlinear modal system. The transformed equations are advanced using CVODE, a variable-step, variable-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver from the SUNDIALS (Suite of Nonlinear and Differential/Algebraic Equation Solvers) package, with variable-order backward differentiation formulas (BDF), together with a matrix-free scaled preconditioned generalized minimal residual (SPGMR) solver in two dimensions. Systematic one- and two-dimensional convergence studies are performed for chemotactic sensitivities $\chi$ = 1–5 and are complemented by independent conservative finite-volume/method-of-lines solutions in physical space. The finite-volume discretizations exhibit second-order self-convergence and closely reproduce the converged GITT fields. The parametric study quantifies the transition from weak relaxation to strong aggregation and the growth of genuinely two-dimensional mixed modes. For $\chi$ = 5, successive truncations up to 7,920 spatial modes (15,840 coupled ODEs) resolve a strongly localized regime. Physical and spectral localization scales contract consistently, while normalized profiles collapse onto an approximately invariant shape. Independent late-time extrapolations yield characteristic times clustered near $t$ $\approx$ 2.184. The results demonstrate a high-resolution hybrid framework for nonlinear coupled-field partial differential equation (PDE) systems with cross-field transport, evolving localization, and demanding multiscale resolution, while providing numerical evidence compatible with possible finite-time singularization without constituting a mathematical proof of blow-up.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Complex and multiphysics engineering systems are frequently governed by interacting transport fields in which one variable modifies the flux, source, stability, or spatial organization of another. Such structures occur in reactive and chemically influenced transport, thermo-fluid and electrochemical systems, micro-scale transport, and other coupled-field models. Despite the diversity of applications, these systems share recurring numerical difficulties: nonlinear feedback, conservation constraints, stability transitions, strong localization, and the emergence of progressively finer spatial scales. Reliable computation therefore requires not only stable time integration but also transparent control of spatial resolution and independent verification of the interacting fields.

Although introduced in mathematical biology, Keller–Segel chemotaxis provides a particularly transparent representative of this broader class of nonlinear coupled-field transport problems. Cell density evolves by diffusion and by a directed flux driven by gradients of a second field, while the chemoattractant itself diffuses, is produced by the cell population, and decays. The resulting two-way feedback loop couples transport, reaction, and field-induced drift and can trigger instability, pattern formation, and sharp localization. In its biological setting, chemotaxis is the directed migration of cells or microorganisms in response to chemical cues and is involved in processes such as bacterial nutrient search, immune-cell recruitment, tissue organization, wound healing, and developmental cell migration. From a computational perspective, however, the same mathematical structure makes the Keller–Segel system a demanding benchmark for methodologies intended for complex coupled transport and multiphysics models.

The mathematical foundations of continuum chemotaxis modeling can be traced to the work of Patlak [1] and to the seminal models introduced by Keller and Segel [2], [3]. Since then, Keller–Segel-type systems have become a central framework for studying the competition between random cell diffusion and directed chemotactic drift. Reviews by Horstmann [4], [5] and Hillen and Painter [6] document the extensive mathematical development of these models and their many variants. Even in their minimal forms, Keller–Segel systems can exhibit a remarkably rich spectrum of behavior, including aggregation, spatial patterning, spike formation, traveling structures, stabilization, and, for suitable parameter ranges and model classes, finite-time concentration or blow-up phenomena [7], [8], [9].

These same nonlinear mechanisms make Keller–Segel systems demanding computational problems. The numerical representation of aggregation must simultaneously preserve global quantities, maintain physically admissible solutions, and resolve progressively steeper spatial gradients. A broad range of discretization strategies has therefore been developed, including finite-volume schemes [10], positivity-preserving finite-volume/finite-difference formulations [11], [12], adaptive moving-mesh methods [13], and multidimensional difference-potential algorithms [14]. Accurate computation becomes particularly delicate when a localized peak narrows rapidly, since a numerically stable time integration does not by itself guarantee adequate spatial resolution. For blow-up-like solutions, the convergence of the computed concentration time is itself a nontrivial issue [15].

A central numerical question in strongly aggregative regimes is therefore not only whether a discrete solution can be advanced in time, but also whether the spatial representation remains resolved as increasingly high wavenumbers become dynamically relevant. This distinction is especially important in two dimensions, where localized concentration can transfer progressively more information toward the upper end of a spectral representation. Under such conditions, low-order observables may appear converged while peak height and width remain sensitive to spatial truncation. Reliable interpretation consequently requires complementary diagnostics that monitor physical-space localization, spectral-space resolution, and agreement with an independently converged numerical methodology.

Despite these advances, the numerical literature considered here remains dominated by physical-space discretizations in which spatial resolution is controlled through mesh refinement. In strongly localized Keller–Segel dynamics, this makes it difficult to monitor directly how nonlinear interactions redistribute content across spatial scales, while independent verification is commonly performed within closely related discretization frameworks. The methodological gap addressed here is therefore a multidimensional transform formulation that (i) treats the spatial means analytically, (ii) evaluates the two-dimensional nonlinear modal couplings exactly rather than by numerical quadrature, (iii) exposes a sparse interaction structure whose truncation can be monitored directly in spectral space, and (iv) is independently verified against a converged conservative physical-space method. To the authors’ knowledge, this combination of exact sparse Generalized Integral Transform Technique (GITT) coupling, systematic one- and two-dimensional modal convergence, independent finite-volume method (FVM)/Method of lines (MOL) verification, and high-resolution physical–spectral localization diagnostics has not previously been developed for the parabolic–parabolic Keller–Segel benchmark considered here.

Within this context, the GITT provides an alternative hybrid numerical–analytical framework. GITT combines eigenfunction expansions with numerical integration of the transformed ordinary differential equation (ODE) system, thereby retaining an analytical representation of the spatial dependence while controlling approximation through modal truncation. Recent applications by independent groups [16], [17] complement the broader computational–analytical GITT framework developed for linear and nonlinear transport problems [18], [19], [20]. This structure is attractive for Keller–Segel systems because spatial convergence can be examined directly in modal space, while nonlinear field coupling can be treated without discretizing the partial differential equation (PDE) itself on a conventional physical-space mesh. More generally, these features are valuable in coupled engineering transport models for which interaction mechanisms and resolution transfer between spatial scales must be monitored explicitly.

The present work treats the parabolic–parabolic Keller–Segel model both as a chemotaxis system and as a canonical nonlinear coupled-field transport problem within a broader multiphysics modeling context. A multidimensional GITT formulation with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions is developed in which the spatially averaged components are separated and treated analytically, so that only zero-mean fluctuations are represented through the eigenfunction expansion. In two dimensions, a tensor-product Neumann basis is employed and nonlinear modal interactions are evaluated by exact cosine-product selection rules. This produces a highly sparse transformed system despite the large number of formally possible mode interactions. The nonlinear ODEs are integrated using variable-order backward differentiation formulas (BDF) through CVODE (a variable-step, variable-order ODE solver from SUNDIALS), with a matrix-free scaled preconditioned generalized minimal residual (SPGMR) linear solver for the multidimensional calculations. The formulation is therefore designed not only to compute the coupled fields but also to expose modal interaction, stability, scale transfer, and localization in a form suitable for systematic verification.

The numerical assessment is deliberately broader than a single high-sensitivity calculation. First, systematic one-and two-dimensional GITT convergence studies are carried out for

Second, the GITT solutions are confronted with conservative finite-volume/method-of-lines formulations developed independently in physical space. These finite-volume solutions are themselves subjected to grid-refinement studies, allowing verification to be based on two separately converged spatial methodologies rather than on a single reference computation. Third, the resulting converged solutions are used for a quantitative parametric analysis of the effect of

in both one and two dimensions, including the growth of genuinely multidimensional mixed harmonics. The independent FVM/MOL comparisons are restricted to the uniformly resolved verification windows (

The strongly aggregative
χ = 5
regime is then followed beyond the uniform parametric window through successive spectral truncations up to 7,920 spatial modes, corresponding to 15,840 coupled ODEs. An outer-shell spectral criterion defines a truncation-dependent resolution frontier. Physical and spectral localization are quantified independently through the full width at half maximum and a root-mean-square wavenumber scale, while normalized profiles test for self-similar collapse. These diagnostics reveal an approximately self-similar concentration regime and provide mutually consistent characteristic-time estimates near
t ≈ 2.184
. The computations therefore furnish strong numerical evidence compatible with possible finite-time singularization, while they are not interpreted as a mathematical proof of blow-up of the continuous PDE system.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the Keller–Segel formulation, spatial-average equations, and zero-mean decomposition. Section 3 develops the one- and two-dimensional GITT formulations and sparse nonlinear modal coupling. Section 4 presents the temporal checks, systematic GITT convergence studies, and independent FVM/MOL verification. Section 5 develops the one- and two-dimensional parametric analysis and quantifies nonlinear multidimensional transfer. Section 6 examines the
χ = 5
high-resolution concentration regime, including the resolution frontier, localization scales, profile collapse, and characteristic-time extrapolation. Section 7 summarizes the principal findings.

sec.title: 4. Numerical implementation, convergence, and independent verification
sec.p: The transformed systems derived in Section 3 are nonlinear initial-value problems whose dimension is controlled by the modal truncation. The numerical strategy adopted here separates temporal accuracy, GITT spatial convergence, and independent physical-space verification. The one-dimensional benchmark is first used for analytical and temporal checks and for a systematic modal-convergence study. The same convergence architecture is then extended to the two-dimensional problem. Finally, both formulations are confronted with conservative finite-volume/method-of-lines (FVM/MOL) solutions obtained directly in physical space.

sec.p: The modal ODEs are integrated with CVODE from the SUNDIALS library using variable-order BDF and adaptive temporal error control. The production tolerances are:

For the one-dimensional GITT benchmark, the transformed system is sufficiently small for a dense Newton/direct linear solve. For the multidimensional calculations, direct factorization becomes impractical as the number of retained modes increases; the production implementation therefore uses matrix-free SPGMR with maximum Krylov dimension 80 and at most 10 restarts. No preconditioner was used over the truncation ranges reported here. All nonlinear modal coefficients are generated once from the exact selection rules of Section 3.4, and only nonzero interactions are stored.

The independent FVM/MOL calculations use the same CVODE tolerances but a completely different spatial representation. The one-dimensional FVM system is solved with a banded direct linear solver, whereas the two-dimensional FVM system uses matrix-free SPGMR because the finest 161 × 161 grid generates 51,842 coupled ODEs. sec.title: 6. High-resolution spectral analysis of the concentration regime
sec.p:
The parametric calculations of Section 5 show that the
χ
= 5 solution enters a rapidly concentrating regime after the initially well-resolved interval. The numerical question then changes qualitatively. It is no longer sufficient to verify convergence of a few low modes or successful completion of the time integrator: the narrowing cell-density structure requires progressively higher spatial wavenumbers. This section therefore combines modal convergence, an outer-shell resolution criterion, physical- and spectral-space localization measures, and scaled-profile analysis. The purpose is to characterize the concentration process without identifying numerical loss of resolution with blowup of the continuous PDE.

sec.p: All four independent extrapolations fall within the narrow interval:

The agreement is noteworthy because the four diagnostics probe different aspects of the calculation: peak amplitude, a physical-space width, a Parseval-consistent spectral length, and the truncation-dependent loss-of-resolution frontier.

Nevertheless, Eq. (125) must be interpreted with care. The computations establish a pronounced blow-up-like concentration regime and provide strong numerical evidence compatible with finite-time singularization, but they do not prove that the solution of the continuous parabolic-parabolic Keller-Segel problem becomes unbounded at that time. A mathematical blow-up statement would require analysis beyond numerical extrapolation, and the fitted exponents may still exhibit pre-asymptotic drift as the concentration scale contracts. The present conclusion is therefore restricted to the numerical evidence: the resolved solution approaches an approximately self-similar, rapidly localizing regime whose independent diagnostic time scales consistently cluster near
t ≈ 2.184
.

sec.title: 7. Conclusions
sec.p: This work developed a multidimensional GITT formulation for a parabolic–parabolic Keller–Segel system, with analytical separation of the spatial means and exact sparse cosine-product coupling in two dimensions. The resulting modal system preserves the mean balances explicitly, exposes nonlinear transfer among retained modes, and provides direct control of spatial truncation within a hybrid numerical–analytical framework.

Systematic one- and two-dimensional convergence studies, together with independent conservative FVM/MOL calculations, verified the transformed solutions over the uniformly resolved comparison windows. The finite-volume discretizations exhibited clean second-order self-convergence, and close agreement with GITT was obtained for both the cell-density and chemoattractant fields. Across
χ = − 1 5
, the parametric analysis captured the transition from weak relaxation to strong aggregation and quantified the growth of genuinely two-dimensional mixed modes.

For
χ = 5
, successive refinements up to 7,920 spatial modes allowed the rapidly concentrating regime to be followed beyond the uniform parametric window. Physical width, spectral localization, outer-shell resolution diagnostics, and normalized-profile collapse consistently indicated an approximately self-similar concentrating state, with independent extrapolations clustering near
t ≈ 2.184
. These observations are compatible with possible finite-time singularization but do not constitute a mathematical proof of blow-up; the late-time estimates remain numerical and may still contain pre-asymptotic drift.

Taken together, the results show that GITT can serve both as a high-accuracy solver and as a spectral diagnostic framework for nonlinear coupled-field transport. The combination of exact modal coupling, independent physical-space verification, and complementary localization measures provides a transferable computational strategy for other complex transport systems. Beyond chemotaxis, the mathematical structure investigated here, involving cross-gradient transport, coupled source and decay mechanisms, stability transitions, and progressive localization, is shared by a broader class of complex multiphysics engineering systems. Future developments may address adaptive modal enrichment, preconditioning at larger transformed dimensions, and extensions to Keller–Segel variants or additional interacting fields.
